items.title: The Strait of Hormuz is largely closed to shipping
summary: On 28 February 2026, war involving Iran led to the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula.

UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) reports that about a third of the world's seaborne fertilizer trade and about a quarter of its seaborne oil normally pass through the strait, and that ship transits fell by about 95% in March.

The World Bank reports that by April 2026 its fertilizer price index had reached its highest level since October 2022. In September 2026, researchers writing for CGIAR reported that fertilizer shipments out of the Persian Gulf remained largely halted.

reach.title: Fertilizer prices
reach.text: Canada mines more potash than any other country and makes much of its own nitrogen fertilizer, but Canadian farmers pay world prices. In March 2026 The Western Producer reported that world urea prices had jumped about 40%. Higher prices raise the cost of next year's crops.

reach.title: Phosphate fertilizer
reach.text: Sulphur from Gulf oil and gas plants is a raw material for phosphate fertilizer, so phosphate prices can rise even where the fertilizer itself is not shipped through the strait.

reach.title: Fuel
reach.text: Higher oil prices feed into diesel for tractors, trucks and trains, and into the cost of moving food.

reach.title: Possible gains
reach.text: Canadian potash and nitrogen producers may sell more abroad at higher prices. Gains and losses will not fall on the same people.

watch.title: Ships through key sea lanes
watch.text: Ships through the Strait of Hormuz averaged 3 a day over the four weeks to 22 November 2026. In the same weeks of the past five years the typical figure was about 83 a day. That is below the range of every one of those years, about 96% below the typical level. Also unusual: Bab el-Mandeb Strait (fewer ships than usual).

watch.title: World fertilizer prices
watch.text: In October 2026, the World Bank's fertilizer price index stood at 148 (2010 = 100), 6% higher than a year earlier. Prices: DAP US$803 a tonne; Urea US$420 a tonne. That is normal for this time of year: it is within the range of the past five years, in US dollars without adjusting for inflation. It is about 8% below the typical level.

watch.title: What farmers pay for inputs
watch.text: In the quarter starting April 2026, the prices Canadian farmers paid for all inputs stood at 187 on Statistics Canada's index (2020 = 100), 11% higher than a year earlier. Fertilizer alone was 24% higher. That is higher than at this time of year in any of the past five years. It is about 20% above the typical level. Worth watching. One unusual reading does not mean a crisis.

watch.title: Diesel prices
watch.text: Diesel at self-serve pumps averaged 262.9 cents a litre across five cities in October 2026, 71% more than a year earlier. That is higher than at this time of year in any of the past five years, after allowing for inflation. It is about 51% above the typical level. Worth watching. One unusual reading does not mean a crisis.

watch.title: World food and energy prices
watch.text: In October 2026, the World Bank's food price index stood at 122 (2010 = 100), 15% higher than a year earlier. Energy prices were 89% higher than a year earlier. That is normal for this time of year: it is within the range of the past five years, in US dollars without adjusting for inflation.

watch.title: The Canadian dollar
watch.text: One US dollar cost $1.42 Canadian on average so far in November 2026, 1.0% more than a year earlier. A weaker Canadian dollar makes imported food and farm inputs dearer. That is higher than at this time of year in any of the past five years. It is about 4% above the typical level. Worth watching. One unusual reading does not mean a crisis.

live.label: Ships through the Strait of Hormuz
live.text: Still showing in the data: about 3 ships a day in the four weeks to 22 November 2026, against a typical 83 for this time of year.
